#2117. Arsenal could expose Liverpool’s biggest weakness at Anfield

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal have spent years struggling to impose themselves at Anfield. However, Mikel Arteta could have an opportunity to change that record when his side face Liverpool on Sunday.

The Gunners have often struggled against the physicality of Liverpool on Merseyside. Since Jurgen Klopp took charge, Liverpool have built a reputation for being high pressing, fast, and making their opponents make mistakes.

However, looking at the latest stats, it seems that Liverpool are no longer as physical, meaning that Arsenal could target their weaknesses.

The disparity is stark between the two teams, with Liverpool having run the least distance of any Premier League side this season. Meanwhile, Arsenal are running the most.

If Arteta’s side can capitalise on this and create fast attacks from possession, then they can utilise this to their advantage.

Liverpool have shifted away from their high-octane style associated with much of Klopp’s reign. Arne Slot has slowly moved towards a more possession-based approach, focusing on keeping the ball.

Andoni Iraola looks keen to add more intensity to their pressing. The Reds have had some of the best pressing stats in the Premier League this season (Opta Analyst).

However, they are not getting the desired intensity from the system.

In addition to chasing the opposition when they have the ball, players must quickly recover, cut off passing lanes and return to their defensive positions.

This is where Arsenal might have an opportunity. If they can get past Liverpool’s first line of pressure, they may have space to push forward before the home side can get back into position.

Another area that the Gunners could target is Liverpool’s midfield.

Alexis MacAllister and Ryan Gravenberch are technically gifted and very composed when they have the ball. But neither are a true defensive midfielder, which raises questions over their ability to stop teams playing through the middle.

Arsenal have the players to exploit this. Declan Rice can put in an energetic, physical performance and drive the play forward. Myles Lewis-Skelly provides another option who can run with the ball into dangerous areas.

This can cause problems for the Liverpool midfield. Arsenal can try to disrupt Mac Allister and Gravenberch, not letting them set the tempo of the game.

If they win these individual battles, it can stop Liverpool from getting the ball control they want.

The task is certainly a tall one. Arsenal have lost their last 16 games at Anfield, including seven in Arteta’s reign.

Whilst that may be the case, the current Liverpool team are very different to the one Arsenal have faced on a regular basis during Klopp’s time in charge.

They certainly can’t expect to be outplayed, but they must take advantage of Liverpool’s failings.

Arsenal are currently second in the Premier League with 21 points from eight games. They will want to win here but will need to do more than just run them into the ground.

If Rice and Lewis-Skelly can push forward and pressurise them, forcing them to make mistakes, then Arteta could finally have his winning recipe at Anfield.

#2116. Arsenal news: Arsenal vs Liverpool. Arteta targets Anfield record as Liverpool prepare for Premier League clash

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal vs Liverpool: Arsenal travel to Anfield on Sunday looking to maintain their strong start to the Premier League season and end a long wait for victory at Liverpool’s home ground.

A blistering start to the season has seen Mikel Arteta’s side win seven of their first eight league games, leaving them tied on points with Manchester City at the top of the table and six points ahead of Liverpool going into the game.

However, the Gunners have not beaten Liverpool in the Premier League at Anfield since 2012/13. Arteta will be aware that the Reds are starting to gel under Andoni Iraola.

They have won three of their last four league games after a lacklustre start and had their first league win at home this season with their 2-0 win over Brighton.

After replacing Arne Slot over the summer, Iraola brought his impressive three-year spell at Bournemouth to Anfield. However, Liverpool have struggled to adjust to the new manager, losing 3 of their first 4 league games.

But they have recently improved and are looking to play a much faster style of football. As Adrian Clarke notes, they are pressing more, not sitting back as much and wanting to attack quickly when they win the ball.

They have been the most direct attackers in the Premier League. They have pace to spare within their attack, with players like Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo providing a threat in advanced areas.

Isak comes into the game in good form after finding the back of the net six times in his first eight league games. He has scored in three successive games in the Premier League for the first time since joining the club.

Florian Wirtz will also play a key role in Liverpool’s attacking play. The German has been consistently creating chances for the team playing behind Isak in a 4-2-3-1 system. He has created nine chances against Brentford.

Arsenal will need to limit the space available to Liverpool’s forward players. Allowing Isak and Gakpo to combine freely could make an already difficult away fixture even harder.

Arsenal have had some positive news on their squad ahead of their Merseyside trip. Declan Rice and Riccardo Calafiori are both back in training.

Christos Tzolis has also trained after missing October. Noni Madueke has also not been ruled out by Arteta ahead of Sunday’s match after he missed the Fleetwood game.

They also have their own fitness issues to contend with. Iraola confirmed that Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Munoz are both available after suffering injuries earlier in the month.

Jeramie Frimpong will be missing due to a hamstring issue but should be back after the international break. Hugo Ekitike, Geovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley are all still sidelined with longer-term injuries.

The presence of Rice will be key for Arsenal. He has been one of the best progressive midfielders in the Premier League, along with their captain, Martin Odegaard.

Despite losing just one of their last eight Premier League clashes against Liverpool, Arsenal are not as strong on the road.

The Gunners have not won any league games in their last 13 trips to Anfield. They have drawn five and lost eight. Their last win was a 2-0 victory back in the 2012/13 season.

They have also never gone 14 games unbeaten away from home in the league. That would be a great achievement.

However, there is good reason to believe they can do it. They have only conceded five clean sheets in the league this season. They have faced the least number of shots on target and the fewest expected goals.

Liverpool have also been on a strong run defensively with four clean sheets in their last six league games, so Arsenal must make their chances count.

A win would provide another key result against a direct rival, improving their position at the top of the Premier League table and finally putting an end to one of the clubs’ longest-running away day woes.

#2115. West Ham 1 – 3 West Bromwich Albion | Final whistle, first impressions in Halloween horror show

Remembrance day at London Stadium. West Ham had good cause to celebrate the absence of VAR in this division in the first few minutes as Mukasa’s dreadful lunge and an Engels clumsy hand ball both went un-noticed and unpunished inside their own penalty box or else the Hammers may have been behind with the first ten minutes once again.

Remembrance Day appropriately marked at London stadium

With young Airidas Golambeckis starting in place of Mavropanos, you sensed the home crowd would be hugely relieved to see out the first half without conceding: Max Kilman getting a yellow card for an unsightly lunge on 16 minutes only adding to the Hammers’ sense of back-line jeopardy.

Whether that yellow card caused Kilman to drop off more – who can say – but almost inevitably, another few minutes was all it took for Albion to take the lead thanks to the Irons’ lazy, loose defending, allowing their opponents to play through them once again with a simple tap in finish following good WBA build up play.

Could have been worse, in truth, as there was almost a second a couple of minutes later as the ball flew just over Hermansen’s bar.

Fortunately, West Ham had Jarrod Bowen to rely on to try and pull them out of the brown smelly stuff: Beating his full back on the outside he fired in a deflected low shot with his weaker foot, to bring the Irons back into a game they had no right to be on level terms in at 30 minutes.

Bowen’s first involvement of the game finding the Baggies’ net. And that was how the half finished with a couple of scares at both ends. No changes at the break – which in itself was a surprise.

More pathetic defending and the Baggies were immediately back in front after the restart. Engles and Kilman between them failing to land a challenge on Jimmy-Jay Morgan who slotted past Hermansen from the left. All that half-time talk gone out of the window inside two minutes. West Ham needed to react immediately so the whole stadium demanded – where were the changes, Nuno?

Piroe and Solomon for Mukasa and Pablo was Nuno’s response on the hour mark. Walker-Peters went close as the chances racked up. West Ham eighth as things stood on 66′. Worse followed as Walker Peters popped a thigh muscle, forcing Nuno to bring Joel Veltman back ahead of schedule, along with Soucek and Castellanos at the same time – Kantė and Golambeckis departing. All five changes made with 20 minutes to go.

Despair in the crowd. And on this keyboard. More boos. Nuno stood, static, deep in thought as another modest opponent was made to look like a table-topper thanks to his line up, his tactics and some terrible defending. Max Kilman – and his manager – are going to cop another shedload of criticism for this effort. West Ham’s third London stadium  loss of the season and six goals conceded in two consecutive home games. Managers have been fired for less.

#2114. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Yes they can. But it’s a longish shot from Gittens that is easily saved by Hamzi in the JDT goal.

More niggle in this match that hasn’t really had many tough challenges. After a few handbags the referee takes control and the argy bargy peters out.

It’s the least the hosts deserve. They have a free-kick 25 yards out, Arribas takes it with his right it’s at the wall but in turning away from the ball Delap deflects it into the far-right corner giving Slonina no chance.

Fluky goal but the hosts have deserved their bit of luck.

Delap again with the goal, this time he goes low, but still to the keeper’s right.

Penalty for Chelsea. Gittens cuts back in the box onto his right and is clipped by the defender. Clear-cut penalty.

Half-chance for Delap on the edge of the area. He playes a one-two with Jackson before opening up his body and letting fly, the shot going well wide.

Another good chance for the hosts and it’s not shock to write that it’s come from the industry of Arribas on the right. He fires in a low cross that evades everyone in the box.

Estevao goes down in the box, it looks as though it could well be a penalty but the referee waves play on. The Brazilian is the shown a yellow card for possibly lashing out having not got the decision he wanted.

The hosts have asserted themselves well this half, in much the same way as they did in the first 45 minutes.

Another good chance for the hosts and again it’s all too easy as Zahedi is one-on-one with the keeper. The striker, however, dithers a bit too long and Slonina makes a fine save. JDT have had plenty of chances to add to their sole goal...

Chelsea have had a ragged start to this half.

Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

#2113. Arsenal injury news: Arteta faces selection dilemma ahead of Liverpool clash

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal will have a few key injury updates ahead of their clash with Liverpool on Sunday, but Mikel Arteta still has some tough choices to make in his front line.

Declan Rice, Riccardo Calafiori and Christos Tzolis have returned to training so there is hope they can play in the Premier League clash against Anfield.

Bukayo Saka is still out with a quad injury, but Noni Madueke looks to be fit to go into the final game. Max Dowman is also suspended after Arsenal were unable to overturn his red card suspension after the defeat to Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup.

However, Arteta has some good options to choose from. He can ill afford any more injuries in attack.

Rice’s return will be key after missing the midweek cup clash.

The midfielder was subbed in the win against Everton with a knock. His absence was a blow against Fleetwood.

He trained on Friday. As long as he does another session on Saturday, he will be available. Rice is a big boost for Arsenal in the middle of the park as they face a Liverpool side who have been in good form recently.

Calafiori is also edging closer to a return. The Italian has played in the last seven Premier League games for Arsenal but missed against Everton.

However, he was only on for a short period when he came on as a sub. But he seemed to have an issue. Arteta said that it didn’t seem like a big problem, but they’re taking some caution.

Like Rice, Calafiori trained on Friday and will be able to go to Merseyside if he finishes his session on Saturday.

Tzolis is another possible addition. The winger has missed Arsenal’s last five matches after suffering a hamstring injury while playing for Greece in October.

His latest scan showed encouraging progress, and he has now returned to training. A further successful session would put him in contention for Sunday’s match.

The main issue for Arteta will be his lack of attacking width.

Madueke did not join the squad for the trip to Fleetwood due to an ankle injury sustained in the Everton game. He did not train on Monday, but Arteta has not ruled him out of the game against Liverpool. He will have to finish his session on Saturday.

Dowman is also missing due to suspension. He was sent off in the 1-1 draw against Fleetwood after a challenge from Harrison Neal. His appeal was rejected by the FA, so he will miss the game against Liverpool.

Saka makes it even worse for the Gunners. The England international has a quad injury from the Bayern Munich game and is likely to be out for several weeks.

Arteta confirmed that he will need another scan before there is a clearer timeline for his return but is likely to be out for a long period of time.

William Saliba is still missing from the squad, having aggravated a back injury during his time playing for France at the World Cup this summer.

But the defender has returned to doing one-on-one training on the training ground.

Arsenal will perform an MRI scan to monitor his progress. Arteta has suggested there have been positive signs, and he is expected back in December.

The main talking point will be Rice, Calafiori and Tzolis returning to training ahead of Sunday.

It would give Arsenal a nice boost with all three players fit. Madueke is still a doubt and they have fewer options going forward with Saka and Dowman out.

#2111. West Ham Player Ratings: WHU 1-3 WBA, No Confidence, No Cohesion And No Answers

West Ham suffered another thoroughly miserable afternoon at the London Stadium as West Bromwich Albion exposed the defensive frailties and midfield problems which have become all too familiar under Nuno Espírito Santo. Jarrod Bowen’s excellent first-half equaliser briefly offered some hope, but the Hammers were second best for much of the opening 45 minutes.

What concerns me most is that there’s something inherently wrong with this team which goes far beyond individual players. There’s no confidence, no cohesion and precious little understanding between teammates. We can’t defend properly, we struggle to pass the ball through midfield and we’re painfully slow when opponents attack us.

West Ham did enjoy plenty of attacking possession in the second half, particularly down the wings, but there was very little cutting edge. Meanwhile, West Brom were able to score three avoidable goals. As I’ve said before, this is not bums on seats football that West Ham are playing.

Came out to punch West Brom’s first corner clear, but his handling of another set piece in the second half was dreadful. Completely lost the flight of the ball and West Ham were fortunate not to concede. Another unconvincing afternoon for a goalkeeper whose performances continue to concern me.

Looked sharp going forward and produced some excellent attacking moments, including a lovely pass to release Bowen. Unfortunately, he was repeatedly caught out of position defensively, leaving enormous spaces down West Ham’s right. Kilman and Golambeckis were constantly having to cover for him. Picked up a yellow card and appeared to suffer an injury before being replaced by Veltman.

I was really impressed with the youngster during the opening stages. His reading of the game was excellent, he anticipated danger, won important tackles and showed remarkable composure when turning out of trouble under pressure.

Unfortunately, Jed Morgan got the better of him for West Brom’s second goal, although Austbø’s dreadful pass had created the problem in the first place. Golambeckis recovered to make an excellent block when Isaac Price threatened on the break. A mixed afternoon, but I still think there’s a very promising footballer here.

Airidas Golambeckis was far from West Ham’s worst player.

Probably West Ham’s busiest defender, making several important blocks and interceptions. He repeatedly had to cover the space left by Walker-Peters and produced an excellent intervention to prevent Ousmane Diakité from scoring.

However, he was also involved in the defensive confusion for West Brom’s opening goal and received a deserved yellow card for a rash challenge after stepping into midfield. Almost scored with a header from Bowen’s corner. Did plenty of good things, but was part of a defence that conceded three poor goals.

His involvement in the opening goal wasn’t particularly impressive, with West Brom finding it far too easy to get behind the defence.

But his worst moment came for the third goal. From a West Brom corner, Morato made a complete hash of his clearance, barely flicking his foot at the ball and failing even to get it out of the penalty area. Callum Styles subsequently scored with a half-volley which bounced through a crowd of players. Really poor defending.

An absolutely dreadful performance. Made a mess of two attempted clearances early on, completely missed the ball on one occasion and was repeatedly dispossessed in dangerous areas.

Diakité seemed to have his number, and Engels was beaten far too easily in midfield. His corner delivery was also poor, with one dreadful low effort failing to beat the first man. Picked up West Ham’s third yellow card late on.

Certainly couldn’t fault his effort. Had an early half-volley which went over the bar and another goal-bound attempt deflected behind after excellent work from Austbø.

There were moments when he looked relatively dangerous, and I still think there’s a potentially effective footballer there. However, his partnership with Pablo was thoroughly uninspiring, and West Ham never looked particularly threatening through the middle. Replaced by Souček.

A technically gifted footballer who I think West Ham are wasting in his current role. Far too often, Mukasa was having to drop deep to collect the ball from the centre-backs because there was absolutely no fluidity in midfield.

He should be operating much further forward, where he can influence attacks rather than trying to compensate for everyone else’s inability to move the ball. Had an early moment when he might have conceded a penalty on another day. Replaced by Solomon.

Scored West Ham’s equaliser with a brilliant right-footed finish after driving into the penalty area. It was a desperately needed goal at a time when the Hammers were massively under the cosh.

Looked lively at times, producing some excellent dribbling and a lovely sidestep down the right, although one promising cross was badly overhit. Delivered the corner from which Kilman nearly scored. One of the few players capable of creating something, but even Bowen couldn’t rescue this performance.

Produced some absolutely excellent runs down the left, including a dazzling early slalom into the penalty area which created a shooting opportunity for Kanté.

Indeed, much of West Ham’s attacking threat came from Austbø’s willingness to run at defenders. Unfortunately, his dreadful misplaced pass shortly after half-time gifted West Brom possession and contributed directly to their second goal.

Tried to make amends with further dangerous runs, but that mistake was extremely costly. A real mixture of exciting attacking play and careless possession.

Another thoroughly disappointing performance. Got himself into a promising position after nine minutes but shot wide, and his first touch repeatedly let him down.

Lost possession in dangerous areas, including an incident which led to West Brom threatening to score again. I can’t fault his willingness to work, but there’s simply no pace, fluency or threat in West Ham’s attacking partnership. Replaced by Piroe before the hour.

Replaced Pablo in the 59th minute. Managed to find a gap through a brick wall of West Brom legs to get a shot away in the 76th minute. There was an appeal for handball, although I didn’t think it was one. Offered little else to suggest West Ham were going to find a way back.

Came on for Mukasa and quickly played the ball to Walker-Peters, whose powerful effort forced a good save. However, he couldn’t provide the attacking spark West Ham desperately needed.

Immediately made an important defensive tackle after replacing the injured Walker-Peters, conceding a corner in the process. Brought some defensive awareness, although by that stage West Ham were chasing the game and the tactical changes were doing little to trouble West Brom.

Barely noticed him after he replaced Kanté. West Ham appeared to have almost completely surrendered midfield by this stage, and Souček did very little to change that.

Replaced Golambeckis as Nuno changed the formation, but was almost completely anonymous.

His first notable contribution was an awful, hopeful shot from distance in the 82nd minute. Two minutes later he produced another effort so high that it had a chance of travelling across London and sailing between the posts at Twickenham. A proper Jonny Wilkinson-style hoof.

#2110. Arsenal transfer news: Gunners target Brazilian teenager Eduardo Pape

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal are increasing their interest in Cruzeiro youngster Eduardo Pape.

Despite the fact he has yet to play for the senior side in Brazil, the 17-year-old has attracted interest from a number of clubs. It is understood that Arsenal is keeping an eye on the youngster. Newcastle United and Bayern Munich are also linked with the midfielder.

The move could be a good fit with the Gunners liking to identify young talent early on. However, Pape is still very much in the early stages of his career, and any move would be seen as an investment into his future.

Arsenal are reportedly targeting Pape as a potential signing in 2027. The teenager is valued at around £33m.

Pape has already had previous experience playing for Cruzeiro’s Under-20s. He’s played 32 times and scored three goals and three assists.

He has left a successful headline in junior football as well. Pape has netted six goals in eight matches and strives for a place in the Brazilian U17 World Cup squad.

The tournament gives an opportunity to demonstrate his skills. The scouts will closely monitor the tournament, so any team interested in the player will be able to see his progress.

Of course, not just Arsenal would want to sign him. Clubs like Newcastle and Bayern Munich have already expressed interest in securing him. This is likely to cause a competitive atmosphere.

There is a concern that there hasn’t been any senior-level play from Pape. As he has never played first-team football before. It will be difficult to see how he will adapt to playing in Europe.

The contract is until December 2029, meaning Cruzeiro are in a strong position. There isn’t a huge need for the Brazilian club to rush into any decisions, meaning Pape can get some experience in a comfortable environment before moving abroad.

However, they have been very successful in the past at bringing in young Brazilian players. Gabriel Martinelli was brought in from Ituano as a teenager and has become an important first team player.

It gives us an insight into what Pape could hope to achieve.

It shows that Arsenal are looking further ahead with their recruitment. Whether they make a move for him remains to be seen. Pape will be one to keep an eye on as we approach the 2027 transfer window.

#2109. Arsenal transfer news: Gunners explore loan move for Real Madrid striker Endrick

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal are keeping their options open regarding a January move for Real Madrid striker Endrick, as Mikel Arteta looks to strengthen his attacking options.

The Gunners have been in contact about a loan move for the Brazilian. There is also talk of a permanent move. However, Real Madrid are reluctant to let him leave and feel he has a big future ahead at the club.

Endrick has struggled to earn consistent game time at the Bernabeu.

While he is only 20 years old and has plenty of time left to make his mark at the top level, a new transfer away from Madrid could give him a more consistent role.

Arsenal are among the clubs keeping an eye on Endrick ahead of the January transfer window, reports TEAMtalk.

The forward was loaned to Lyon for the second half of last season to get more regular game time.

However, his representatives are said to be open to looking for another move if things do not improve in Madrid.

It seems Arsenal are interested in signing Endrick on loan with a view to making the move permanent. This will give them time to see how he settles into the Premier League.

However, Real Madrid may be in a strong position. They are still loyal to the young player and would prefer to keep him at the Spanish club.

Arsenal will rely on Madrid being more willing to let him go.

The reported interest from Arsenal comes as Arteta looks to strengthen his attacking options.

Endrick would provide variety to an attacking line-up which has been under pressure of late. His age and potential make a loan deal with an option to make the move permanent an attractive option.

There is also positivity from his previous stint with Lyon. He has already been on a loan move from Madrid and has demonstrated that he can make progress when getting regular game time.

Arsenal have previously signed young talents from Real Madrid.

Martin Odegaard came to north London as a young player after failing to make an impact in the first team at Madrid. He then became a key player for Arteta, taking on the role of captain.

Endrick will be hoping to follow a similar trajectory.

There is no suggestion that any deal is near despite Arsenal’s interest.

Endrick remains an important part of Real Madrid’s long-term plans. His representatives are thought to be looking at other options to help his career develop.

This loan deal would provide a solution for all parties. Arsenal would have another attacker to bring in, Endrick would play more regularly and Madrid would still have an interest in his future.

It will also depend on how willing the Spanish giants are to move their stance before January.

For now, Arsenal are in contact with Endrick as they consider a move. The Brazilian’s future may soon become a topic of interest ahead of the winter transfer window.

#2107. West Ham 1 – 3 West Bromwich Albion | Incompetence rules OK

Eighth in the Championship might not seem too bad to the casual observer. But for a club of the size of West Ham United, expected to boss the division owing to their finances, their huge following and the massive reputations of most of their players and their manager, this is a crisis.

Anyone in the board room who thinks otherwise needs to go and find another sport to waste their money on.

Six goals conceded on consecutive Saturdays at home in the second division. No passion on the pitch. No drive – save for Jarrod Bowen pulling a goal back.

Did anybody care, I wondered, other than the unfortunate tens of thousands who had paid hundreds to watch that largely disinterested group of players run around, orchestrated by an incompetent ‘coach’ on the sidelines who seems to be dreaming of a long holiday paid for by the West Ham board when their patience finally, inevitably snaps after watching a side of this value and cost perform like a team of fourth division misfits.

Disjoined substitutions – playing Soucek as a deep sitting, central midfielder when he should have been camped in the opposition ‘box for the last half an hour  – just don’t make sense. Taking off Mukasa again, West Ham’s most gifted midfielder. No plan.

The only ‘plus’ side was that millions of armchair Hammers fans avoided the pain of watching it live. Go watch the highlights and tell me I’m wrong but that manager, with that starting eleven, should have just ordered his own p45. I’ve been solidly behind Nuno and hate the idea of yet more upheaval but – in the immortal words of the Stranglers:

“Something’s happening and it’s happening right now – You’re too blind to see it – Something’s happening and it’s happening right now – Ain’t got time to wait..I said something better change”

#2106. Nuno’s West Ham Project Is Beginning To Look Fundamentally Flawed

West Ham’s 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion was another deeply disappointing afternoon at the London bio, but I am increasingly convinced that the problems at this football club go far beyond individual players. There is something fundamentally wrong with the way this team is playing, and Nuno Espírito Santo is running out of excuses.

The Hammers were second best for large periods, struggled to retain possession, repeatedly exposed their own defence and looked painfully short of confidence. Jarrod Bowen’s excellent equaliser briefly offered some encouragement, but three avoidable goals and another disjointed performance eventually left home supporters heading for the exits before the final whistle.

What concerns me most is the lack of cohesion. We look like a collection of individuals rather than a properly functioning football team. West Ham cannot defend, cannot consistently pass the ball and look incredibly slow whenever opponents show a little bit of energy or attacking ambition.

West Ham actually started reasonably well, winning a corner inside the opening 20 seconds. However, that early enthusiasm lasted barely a minute before West Brom began taking control.

Arne Engels had a particularly difficult opening ten minutes. He was dispossessed in midfield, struggled with his passing and repeatedly found himself on the wrong side of West Brom’s Ousmane Diakité. At times it looked like a mismatch, with Max Kilman having to step out of defence to compensate for problems in front of him.

There is a much bigger issue here than simply one midfielder having a bad afternoon. West Ham are frequently outnumbered in central areas and struggle to retain possession. Even relatively straightforward passes from deep positions can dissect our midfield and leave enormous gaps between the full-backs and centre-backs.

Divine Mukasa is another example of how badly we are utilising the players available. He is a technically gifted footballer, but spent far too much time dropping deep to collect the ball from the centre-backs. We are wasting his ability by making him come looking for possession rather than getting him further up the pitch to influence the game.

I have previously highlighted the potential of the Engels and Mukasa midfield combination, but there is little evidence of the fluidity and understanding that should be developing between these players.

West Brom deservedly took the lead after 20 minutes when a long ball completely split the West Ham defence. Jimmy-Jay Morgan got in behind Kilman and Morato before squaring for Felix Horn Myhre to score.

It was embarrassingly easy. There was very little ingenuity involved, just one long ball and a complete failure to deal with the danger.

Morgan should have made it two shortly afterwards, blazing over when presented with another excellent opportunity. West Ham were fortunate not to be further behind, and the frustration around the London Stadium was becoming increasingly apparent.

Jarrod Bowen provided a moment of genuine quality on 29 minutes. Advancing into the penalty area, the West Ham captain produced an excellent right-footed finish to make it 1-1.

It was desperately needed because West Ham had been massively under the cosh. Bowen looked lively, showed some lovely footwork and was one of the few players attempting to make things happen.

But make no mistake about it, West Brom were comfortably the better team during that opening half-hour.

There was another important intervention from Kilman to prevent Diakité making it 2-1, while Kyle Walker-Peters occasionally looked dangerous going forward. Unfortunately, his defensive positioning was repeatedly exposing the right-hand side.

West Ham were not playing with anything resembling the authority of a home team. Supporters were becoming increasingly frustrated, and I found myself thinking that this was simply not bums-on-seats football.

The second half could hardly have started worse.

Within two minutes, West Ham had given away possession through a sloppy pass from Edvin Austbø. West Brom worked the ball forward, with Morgan once again getting the better of Airidas Golambeckis before finishing to make it 2-1.

I felt desperately sorry for Golambeckis because he had actually been one of West Ham’s better players during the opening stages. His reading of the game and anticipation had impressed me enormously, and he had produced some excellent one-on-one defending. That said, he did repeatedly drop 5 yards behind his defenders and played the opposition onside too frequently.

There is no escaping the fact that he was beaten for the goal. Equally, Austbø’s careless pass had handed West Brom the opportunity in the first place.

Airidas Golambeckis was far from West Ham’s worst player.

It was another example of a West Ham team that simply isn’t playing with confidence. Players look nervous in possession, passing becomes increasingly careless and mistakes are being punished.

To be fair, West Ham did attack regularly after going behind. Austbø continued to threaten down the left, and there was a noticeable improvement in the amount of possession the Hammers enjoyed in dangerous areas.

The problem was the lack of a cutting edge.

A Jarrod Bowen corner produced a good header from Kilman which was unlucky not to find the net, while Walker-Peters forced an excellent save with a powerful effort from distance after being found by Manor Solomon.

West Ham were getting into promising positions, but there was very little creativity through the middle. Almost all our attacking threat was coming from the wings.

Just as West Ham appeared to be building some pressure, another dreadful defensive error effectively settled the game.

On 72 minutes, West Brom won a corner and Morato made a complete hash of his clearance. Rather than properly getting the ball away, he simply flicked a foot at it, producing virtually no distance and failing even to clear the penalty area.

Callum Styles collected the opportunity and struck a half-volley which bounced through a crowd of players before finding the net.

West Ham had enjoyed plenty of possession in the second half and were not necessarily short of attacking opportunities. But the defensive mistakes were proving catastrophic, and there was precious little evidence of a team capable of mounting a serious comeback.

Once again, when West Ham found themselves chasing a game, Nuno reverted to his familiar solution of introducing three centre-backs.

Kyle Walker-Peters had picked up an injury after being booked, and Joël Veltman came on alongside Tomáš Souček and Taty Castellanos. Nuno reshaped his side, withdrawing Golambeckis.

But it didn’t appear to cause West Brom too many problems. If anything, the visitors were left with plenty of opportunities to attack, while West Ham seemed to almost completely surrender control of midfield.

I struggle to understand what Nuno is trying to achieve with some of these tactical changes. There is a recurring pattern of West Ham falling behind, changing formation and then looking even less convincing as a team.

Souček barely featured, Castellanos was almost anonymous and his two efforts from distance hardly suggested a striker desperate to rescue his team. One particularly ambitious attempt sailed so high it had a better chance of ending up between the posts at Twickenham than troubling the West Brom goalkeeper.

West Ham supporters began streaming out of the London Stadium with ten minutes still remaining.

I don’t believe this can simply be explained away by pointing at individual players. Yes, there were some dreadful performances and some equally dreadful mistakes, but there is something inherently wrong with this team.

We have no confidence and no cohesion. We struggle to pass the ball, we struggle to defend and we look painfully slow. It doesn’t take particularly good opposition to cause us problems. Anyone with a little bit of effervescence or vibrancy seems capable of making life extremely uncomfortable for West Ham.

I cannot fault Pablo and Mohamadou Kanté for their effort, and I suspect Kanté could develop into an effective footballer. But the attacking partnership was thoroughly uninspiring and never looked particularly threatening.

There is also a question about the way Nuno is managing this squad. The constant changes, the formations and the apparent inability to settle on a system are not helping matters. I would genuinely be intrigued to see what another coach could achieve with these players.

West Ham have sold a considerable number of players and rebuilt much of the squad. There is an argument that the manager needs time, but there is also an expectation that a team containing this much Championship quality should be considerably more convincing than this.

The supporters are entitled to expect better.

Plans to improve the atmosphere at the London Stadium with fan zones and dedicated singing sections are all well and good. But if the team is going to play like this, it will be a futile exercise.

We stand on the precipice at the moment. The club, the manager and the players all have serious questions to answer.

And after another afternoon like this, I am not sure any of them have provided particularly convincing answers.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live.
